claims.text: Pre-exposure, untreated Q235 steel naturally has a native iron oxide surface film.
The native iron oxide film effectively suppresses corrosion of Q235 steel in mild environments.
High chloride concentration combined with elevated temperature destabilizes the native oxide film on Q235 steel.
Destabilization of the native oxide film accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
The native iron oxide film acts as a passive barrier that limits ion transport.
Limiting ion transport through the native oxide film suppresses corrosion.
Aggressive chloride ions compromise the integrity of the native oxide film.
Thermal stresses at elevated temperature compromise the integrity of the native oxide film.
Compromising the oxide film promotes localized film breakdown and metal dissolution.
Q235 steel exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl at 50–100°C will have lower charge-transfer resistance than steel held at room temperature with low chloride concentration.
Q235 steel exposed to high chloride and elevated temperature will show altered oxide-layer chemical composition relative to the mild-environment control.
Q235 steel exposed to high chloride and elevated temperature will exhibit higher corrosion rates and greater surface degradation than the mild-environment control.
Room-temperature, low-chloride conditions preserve the native oxide film and result in minimal corrosion.
EIS charge-transfer resistance can be used as an indicator of oxide-film integrity in this study.
Surface roughness and microstructural inhomogeneities may influence oxide-film destabilization and corrosion.
Long-term or cyclic real-world behavior may differ because of environmental factors omitted from the laboratory study.
